text: Two worked problems applying this chapter's tools directly to the Steane code: verifying the commutation condition, and computing a syndrome from a specific injected error.

Take row 2 and row 3 of the Steane code's parity-check matrix. Their entrywise product is 0,0,1,0,0,0,1, and summing those mod 2 gives 2, which is 0 mod 2. That confirms rows 2 and 3 overlap in an even number of positions — exactly 2, positions 3 and 7 — satisfying the self-orthogonality condition the Steane-code construction relies on, verified directly alongside every other row pair including each row with itself.

Now suppose an X error hits qubit 3. By the anticommutation rule, it anticommutes with whichever Z-type stabilizers have a 1 in column 3 of H — reading that column directly gives rows 2 and 3, so the Z-type syndrome is 0,1,1. A Z error on qubit 5 anticommutes with whichever X-type stabilizers have a 1 in column 5, giving syndrome 1,0,1. And an X error on qubit 7, whose column is all 1s, flips every single Z-type stabilizer, giving syndrome 1,1,1.

Notice this column-lookup shortcut never required simulating the full 7-qubit quantum state at all — it's a purely classical lookup, inherited directly from the Hamming 7,4 code's structure. This is the practical payoff of the CSS construction: because the stabilizers are built from a classical parity-check matrix, syndrome computation reduces to classical linear algebra over H, something that scales to much larger codes without ever tracking quantum amplitudes directly.
Next, Chapter 5 takes this exact CSS structure and lays it out on a 2D lattice: the surface code, the leading practical candidate for real fault-tolerant quantum hardware.
